name: Guggul (Commiphora mukul resin extract, by mouth)
short: Multi-ingredient cases: liver failure (transplant) with usnic acid, green tea; hepatitis with red yeast rice. Guggul: 1 rhabdomyolysis case; trial rash; lowered propranolol, diltiazem levels in men.
text: A case report describes rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle breakdown) with haemoglobin in the urine in a 55-year-old man after 2 weeks of a Commiphora mukul extract taken to lower his cholesterol, with very high creatine kinase and raised liver enzymes; all tests returned to normal after he stopped it, and the authors rate guggul a possible cause. In a placebo-controlled trial in 103 adults with high cholesterol, 6 participants given guggulipid (in two dose groups of 33 and 34) developed a hypersensitivity rash compared with none of 36 on placebo, and the authors say guggulipid appeared to cause this skin reaction in some patients. In a 43-person placebo-controlled trial, 10 guggul users versus 4 on placebo reported side effects: mild gastrointestinal discomfort (7), possible thyroid problems (2) and a generalised skin rash (1) that led to withdrawal. In a 61-patient trial, side effects were headache, mild nausea, belching and hiccups in a few patients. In a 90-person placebo-controlled trial of guggul combined with triphala, 2 people on the combination (4.3%) developed a hypersensitivity rash, compared with none on placebo. A case report describes hives-like (urticarial) rashes in a patient taking an Ayurvedic guggulu preparation, which recurred when it was used again; the abstract does not list the preparation's ingredients. A 2005 review concludes that guggul may cause stomach discomfort or allergic rash as well as other serious side effects and interactions, and says it should be avoided in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children. Liver injury (multi-ingredient products only; none of these is data on guggul alone): a case report describes a young, healthy woman with fulminant liver failure who needed an emergency liver transplant, caused by a dietary supplement and fat burner containing usnic acid, green tea and guggul tree extracts; no other cause was found, and the authors place the case among reports of liver toxicity from supplements containing usnic acid while saying that green tea or guggul tree extracts may not be free of adverse effects. Another case report describes acute hepatitis in a 63-year-old woman whose liver enzymes rose severely over a few weeks; for six months she had been taking a lipid-lowering product containing guggulsterol and red yeast rice extract. A liver biopsy showed severe inflammation, liver tests returned promptly to normal after the product was stopped, and the episode was judged an adverse drug reaction after other causes were excluded. The authors note that red yeast rice contains monacolin K, which is identical to lovastatin, a medicine that had earlier caused mild liver toxicity in her. Case reports also name Kanchnar guggulu, a multi-herb Ayurvedic product (described in one report as containing 10 plant extracts; the abstracts do not list them or say whether they include Commiphora mukul), named with another Ayurvedic product in one case report and as the product taken by one of three patients with acute liver injury and jaundice in a case series (each took a different product), all of whom recovered. Two reports, available as titles only, describe allergic contact dermatitis from guggul in creams applied to the skin. Interactions: in a randomised crossover study in healthy men (10 given propranolol, 7 given diltiazem), a single dose of guggul extract significantly lowered blood levels of both medicines, and the authors warn this could reduce their effect. In laboratory studies, guggulsterones activated a receptor that induces CYP3A drug-metabolising genes in human liver cells, and the authors advise caution with medicines metabolised by CYP3A; the same study found that guggulsterones also activated the oestrogen receptor alpha and the progesterone receptor, which the authors say needs further study; in rats, a guggulipid extract increased blood levels of rosuvastatin, and a multi-herb guggul formulation and guggulsterones inhibited CYP3A4. These are laboratory and animal data.
